creator_display_ssim: McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research (estab. 1935, closed 1998), collector
description_tsim: Twenty two subfossil mandibles from Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii). The majority are almost complete, while a few comprise small fragments. The mandibles have been coated in wax; a museum technique of the early to mid-20th century used to stabilise fragile bones. These specimens were collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 6th 1937 to January 26th 1938.
A plaster model of the liver mounted on a wooden stand. Some of the structures have been labeled.
Plaster model of cross-section through the abdomen. Liver, gall bladder, stomach (body), kidneys, inferior vena cava shown when viewed caudally. One of a series of five.
Plaster model of a chimpanzee (Pan sp.) brain.

Oversized hemi (half) head showing the course of cranial nerves. Mounted on a circular wooden base base. A product of Maison Tramond, of Paris, makers of some of the most exquisite and accurate anatomical models of the late 19th and early 20th century. Wax was a favoured material in nineteenth century practices of anatomical model making, both for its malleability and resemblance to human flesh.

Plaster cast of a partial mandible from a human (Homo sp.), probably prehistoric. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in c. 1900 to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

Fossils of fish vertebrae (30) and fragments of turtle shell (3) contained in a black cardboard box with a glass top. The fossils are stained a dark chocolate brown colour. Similar in appearance to fossils from the Eocene oil shale deposits of Gladstone, Queensland.
Ulna from a species of large, flying bird, probably an albatross (Family Diomedeidae).

description_tsim: Subfossil tibia from a long-nosed potoroo (Potorous tridactylus). creator_display_ssim: McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research (estab. 1935, closed 1998), collector
description_tsim: Right half of subfossil mandible of a common wombat (Vombatus ursinus). The mandible has been coated in wax; a museum technique of the early to mid-20th century used to stabilise fragile bones. This specimen was collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 6th 1937 to January 26th 1938. In 1802, the log books of the sailing ship the Lady Nelson recorded the existence of wombats on King Island, but the Field Naturalists’ Club of Victoria failed to find any during their 1887 visit, suggesting that the species went extinct on the island some time before the beginning of the twentieth century.
Left mandible of domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris). Two molars present.

Skull, no mandibles, of a Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii). Skull is bisected sagittally along the midline. Left section is covered in blotchy stains and missing part of the front of the maxilla.
Left half skull section of a domestic sheep or goat. No maxilla or mandible.

description_tsim: Plaster cast of a right first metatarsal from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis). This bone was part of a fossil assemblage discovered in Krapina, Croatia between 1899 and 1905. These Neanderthal fossils have been dated at 120-130 thousand years old and represent one of the largest assemblages of Upper Pleistocene human skeletal remains ever found. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in the early 1900s to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

creator_display_ssim: Dr Herman Fermor Lawrence (b.1863, d.1936), maker
credit_line_tsim: Gift of Dr Herman Lawrence, 1919-1920
description_tsim: This early 20th century wax moulage depicts a young Middle Eastern girl suffering from Molluscum contagiosum, a non-fatal viral infection. One of the risk factors of this virus is crowded living conditions, and as an immigrant to Melbourne at this time, it is very likely this girl was experiencing such conditions. This moulage was created by Dr Herman Lawrence, the first dermatologist of Melbourne’s St. Vincent’s Hospital.  Lawrence was following the lead of European moulage makers in giving his waxes realistic details like eyebrows, eyelashes and accurate skin tone. In this era, a wax cast was one of the only ways to accurately document in three dimensions the external symptoms of disease. Lawrence donated his moulages to the University of Melbourne in 1919-1920.
Multilayered calculus embedded in a resin block.

Calculus specimen sectioned in half, polished. A calculus is a concretion of material, usually mineral salts, that forms in an organ or duct of the body. The concentric, radial in this calculus means it is likely a kidney stone formed from uric acid.

creator_display_ssim: Department of Pathology, University of Melbourne, maker
description_tsim: 451 page register of specimens added to the Harry Brookes Allen Museum of Pathology from June 1954 to May 1964 (1963 is incomplete). Each page has a column for registration number, doctor name, date, description, patient name or details, whence obtained, and disposal, although not all records have all of these details completed. The registration number is a 1-4 digit serial number followed by a forward slash with the last two digits of the year. The registration numbers can be correlated with specimens listed in the 1960 Pathology Museum catalogue in, 'The Melbourne School of Pathology; Phases and Contrasts' book. This register dates from the era before the merger of the Pathology Museum and the Anatomy Museum. At this time, the Harry Brookes Allen Museum of Pathology was located in the Old Pathology Building, now named the Elisabeth Murdoch Building.

Tan leather doctor's bag with carry handle, snap clasp, removable cotton lining with pockets and adjustable leather belt for securing items inside.  Original owner and period of use unknown.    This item became saturated when the Archives Department was flooded (by tap water) in June 2009.  It was immediately taken to The Centre for Cultural Materials Conservation at The University of Melbourne for conservation.  It is consequently now stiffer than before and should be stored and displayed open to prevent putting stress on the folded ends.  The blackend leather at the ends and the tag are the result of water damage to areas of leather suffering red rot.

Whirling Travelette Spray described by manufacturer as: "A scientifically designed and constructed combined spray and enema syringe". Manufacturer's details are on the box lid:  "AJAX BRAN, ARTHUR H HUMPHREY & CO MELBOURNE".  Syringe has a large red rubber bulb and a vulcanite nozzle. It is in its original box with instructions.  Date range unknown, but box has price on it (24/9) indicating prior to 1966.
Early model stethoscope with white rubber ear plugs, black neck straps, brass binaural piece, and a wood chest piece.
Hinged folding tongue depressor. Engraved "WD 5 SICK BAY RWH". Possibly nickel plated brass.
Glass 1cc syringe with glass plunger and stainless steel needle.

Stainless steel kidney dish, engraved "BTS" (Blood Transfusion Service). The following manufacturer's details are stamped into the base: "STAINLESS / STEEL / BY / PARAMOUNT / K.G. LUKE / MELB / S4". Typical of those used for many years at the women's hospital and for many purposes.

Ward side trolley from the old gynaecology wards at the Royal Women’s Hospital site which was demolished pre 1970. The trolley is made of seamless steel tubing, enamelled light cream, and has four steel capped rubber-tyred castors attached to the feet.  It has tubular metal legs, a thin tubular metal stretcher, and a flat single sheet metal top. As seen in photographs from early 20th century.

Large glass and steel syringe with leur lock, glass barrel, glass plunger, metal hub and 3 metal finger rings, one on either side of the barrel and one on the plunger. The syringe barrel has brown markings graduated from 1.0 to 10 cc and the manufacturer's details in brown: "TRADE VAN MARK".

Thought to be a portable ether anaesthesia and analgesia machine in purpose-made wood box. Box is painted cream and has a hinged lid and a single catch at the front. The box may have had a handle at some stage as two metal attachments are still present on the side of the box. The set includes what is thought to be a metal ether inhaler drum which is circular and attached to the floor of the case. There are lengths of corrugated rubber hose with connectors,  brittle and perishing, there is a glass ether bottle and a rebreathing bag. The top of the drum has a control level for with increments from 0, ¼, ½, ¾.. The glass jar has a screw top lid and an inner metal canisters. There are three metal connectors attached to the metal lid. The lid is stamped "G Kaye 44". The rebreathing bag has an angled connector which is also stamped: "G Kaye 44". G Kaye is thought to refer to Melbourne-born anaesthetist Geoffrey Kaye (1903-1986) who had his own engineering works and who may have originally built this piece. The item is very similar to Dr Thomas Small's portable ether inhaler.
Bakelite rectal tube with four holes at the end. The pipe would be attached to tubing, which was attached to the douche reservoir and used for rectal douche or enemas.

Circa 1880s Women's Hospital nurse's uniform skirt made from a fine vertical blue and white striped cotton, it has a full length gathered skirt with waistband, a back opening secured by two hook and eyes and one press stud. It is machine made with some hand stitching. Attached to the skirt is a white cotton label with "Royal Women's Hospital" in blue cotton. The uniform includes a shirt A1990_24_002, apron A1990_24_003, armband A1990_24_004, cap A1990_24_005, large collar A1990_24_006, and two additional caps A1990_24_007 and 008.  Notes accompanying the item suggest that it is unclear whether this item is an original uniform or a facsimile created in the mid twentieth century. Further research is required to confirm this.

Nurse’s certificate issued to Joan Stevens by "The Women’s Hospital and Alfred Hospital Combined Training School for Nurses". The certificate reads: "Melbourne 10.5.45 / This is to Certify that / Joan Stevens / has been trained at these Hospitals for three years in Medical, Surgical / and Gynaecological Nursing and has attended the prescribed course of lectures, has passed the prescribed examinations and is qualified to be registered as a trained General Nurse."  The certificate is signed by the Hospital President, Chairman Honorary Medical Staff, Matron, Manager & Secretary of both hospitals. Not signed by Joan Stevens  The certificate is on cream paper and mounted and presented in a brown leatherette folder with gold embossed borders. The text is printed in black ink and signatures are in black and blue ink. The title is embossed in gold on the front of the folder: "NURSE’S CERTIFICATE".  23.5 x 16.3cm (closed), 32.5 x 23.5cm (open).

Printed certificate. The certificate reads: "Women’s Hospital / And / Infirmary for Diseases Peculiar to Women / Melbourne. / This is to certify that / has received Instruction in the Special work of the Gynaecological / and Midwifery Department of this Hospital for a period of / months, and, after / due examination, was found to be competent to discharge the / duties of a Gynaecological and Midwifery Nurse."  There is space for it to be signed by the Hospital President, Honorary Secretary, Lady Supt., Examiners and House Surgeons and the nurse. Printed by Modern Printing Co. PTY. Stainless steel canister with perforations on top and screw cap on base for replacing powder. Before disposable surgical gloves were introduced, gloves had to be washed and autoclaved before re-use. Canvas pouches (five) used when weighing premature babies by domiciliary nurses. description_tsim: Tool used for pouring molten metal in the casting process, in dentistry the  procedure provided a metallic duplication of missing tooth structure with as much accuracy as possible. Most likely the casting method used was lost-wax process, also called cire-perdue, a method of metal casting in which a molten metal is poured into a mold that has been created by means of a wax model. Once the mold is made, the wax model is melted and drained away. The lost wax technique is also common practice in jewellery.  Owned by John Samuel Robert Heath (1893-1970) Dentist, surgeon and artist. Heath joined the Medical Corps, and saw service in Egypt, Gallipoli and France, being mentioned in dispatches for bravery and awarded the 1914/15 Starr, the British War Medal and the Victory Cross. He returned to Australia after studying dentistry at Royal Dental Hospital in Leicester Square, London. Honorary Dental Surgeon to the Melbourne Dental Hospital and the Childrens Hospital, Melbourne; Dentist to the Children's Welfare Department Deports, Royal Park; Director of the Malocclusion Clinic, Melbourne Dental Hospital; Lecturer and Examiner in Orthodontia, the University of Melbourne; formerly House Surgeon and Demonstrator in Operative Dental Surgery, the Royal Dental Hospital, London: and Special Magistrate of the Children's courts.

description_tsim: Brass engraved plaque with black lettering affixed to wooden backing. It was created to indicate that the x-ray machine alongside which it stood was installed by the Melbourne Dental Students' Society in 1923 to perpuate the memory of those students who fell during World War I.  In spite of repeated requests from the Dental Students’ Society for an X -ray machine and lectures on dental radiography, neither the Australian College of Dentistry nor the Hospital had, after the First World War, the means to provide these essential teaching and service requirements.   In the early 1920s the students took the matter into their own hands and raised the necessary funds to purchase a machine and to arrange for a practitioner to give lectures. As a permanent record this plaque was fixed to the wall of the X-ray department in the Australian College of Dentistry at 193 Spring St where it remained until removed in 1962 for transfer to the new accommodation in what was then ‘the new Dental Hospital and School’ on Elizabeth Street. It was ‘lost’ during the move and not recovered until 1993 when another ’new building’ was already being considered.

description_tsim: The equipment can be divided into four parts; a dental component, an electric motor, a stand, and foot a control. The dental component consists of a standard cable arm with slip joint and a straight handpiece driven by a cord belt from a countershaft mounted below the motor. This section of the engine has seen little change in overall design since the 1860s. The stand is ornate cast iron with a circular top and four legs each fitted with a fixed wheel, not a caster, making free movement difficult. The top has a circular polished wooden disc to which the motor is attached with below, a countershaft, pulleys and electric clutch. Attached the polished wood disc is an oval brass plate. A cord drive from the motor goes to the clutch which, in the "out” position, allows it to run without turning the hand piece. The motor is double wound with both consummator for power and slip rings to supply a low voltage to instruments for use in the mouth. All enclosed in a metal cover. The foot control consists of a very large, heavy attachment giving a speed control in both forward and reverse. It is used also to “open” the clutch to allow the motor to run as a generator without turning he drill.  From the first introduction of an electric supply America had favoured an alternating source (A.C.) whereas Great Britain had direct current ( D.C.) The SSW Co could have solved the problem of a safe low voltage by installing a transformer.

description_tsim: This is a copy of the early microscope made by Antonj van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) in the latter part of the 1600s in the Netherlands. The simple instrument uses one lens, mounted in a hole in the brass plate that makes up the body of the apparatus. The specimen is mounted in front of the lens, on the sharp point that sticks up at the front of the apparatus, its position and focus adjusted by turning the two screws. The specimen is viewed through the lens by holding the device in the hand, close to the eye. The initial observations of oral bacteria within dental plaque were made by van Leeuwenhoek using his primitive microscopes in 1680, an event recognized as the advent of oral microbiological investigation.  The  microscope was a gift to the University of Melbourne in September 1974 from Professor Carl de Gruchy. A 1944 Melbourne Medical alumnus, Professor de Gruchy was a Beaney scholar in 1946 and took out his Doctor of Medicine degree in 1948. His early days spent at St Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne were followed by postgraduate work in London and a Rockefeller Fellowship in the USA. He  returned to Melbourne in 1952 and began a distinguished career specialising in haematology, based at St Vincent's and the University of Melbourne. He retired from the chair of medicine at St Vincent's in 1970.

description_tsim: Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid.  The collection of sterio skiagrams is Fryett's work in the Anatomy department, University of Melbourne from 1902 to c. 1914.

Collection of slides from a large personal collection of  Dr R.J. Wright-Smith (1898-1946), pathologist Royal Melbourne Hospital 1928-1946. There is a mixture of human and animal tissue (rat), the majority is human tissue. The collection includes slides from institutions all over the world, including  places such as Leeds, Manchester, Glasgow, New York, Cape Town, and Hong Kong.  Redford Wright-Smith  commenced his medical course at King's College, London at the end of the War, and completed his studies with high honours at Melbourne University in 1924. He was appointed resident medical officer at the Melbourne Hospital and was a registrar the next year. Having obtained the degree of MD in 1927 he turned to pathology, first as a resident and later as non-resident pathologist  During the war years and in the new hospital site in Parkville his interest in teaching developed, leading to the establishment of a weekly demonstration of interesting specimens and discussion of the clinical features of the cases. This set a pattern for `Friday lunch-time' which has continued for forty years.  He assisted Dr CH Mollison as coroner's surgeon and later succeeded him as government pathologist. He had a unique experience of nearly 20,000 personally conducted autopsies and established a high reputation in both medical and legal circles as an expert witness in forensic and medico-legal cases. In 1943 he succeeded Dr Mollison as lecturer in forensic medicine at the University of Melbourne.

Reprinted from: The Medical Journal of Australia August 20,  1960, pp. 297-299.  Dr Vera Isabella Krieger (1901-1992) was a trailblazer in women’s health and has left an impressive legacy. Doctor of Science of the University of Melbourne. Krieger entered the University of Melbourne in 1921, graduating BSc in 1927 and MSc in 1927. In 1938 conferred for DSc In 1926 Vera Krieger became a research bio-chemist and assistant to Dr Robert Marshall-Allen, Director of Obstetrical Research and the first Professor of Obstetrics at the University of Melbourne in1929 On the 1st of May1928, Dr Krieger was appointed as the Royal Women Hospital's first clinical biochemist where she continued to work until retirement in 1968. All her work was carried out in the Biochemistry Department at the University of Melbourne by agreement with W J Young, Associate Professor of Biochemistry and W J Osbourne, the Professor of Physiology. Her research contributed to a better understanding of many serious health conditions. She helped save countless lives.  Dr Krieger was particularly interested in high blood pressure during pregnancy. She was also keen to understand spontaneous recurrent miscarriages.  Her most important work was in the field of Rhesus immunisation.

description_tsim: Part of a set of three illustrations relating to surgery for pre auricular lymphadenitis (MAIS), prepared for three-colour printing. These beautiful illustrations show the surgical treatment of first and second branchial cleft anomalies.  Professor John Hutson AO writes of this fiscula as, 'connected to the auditory canal, and requires careful surgery to avoid damaging the facial nerve'. The illustrations are a classic product of their time, being expertly done by Eric Thake (1904–1982), printmaker, photographer and official war artist, in around 1960. They are not only beautifully drawn, but also demonstrate a style of surgery very close to formal dissection. This is in stark contrast to current principles of surgery, where we strive to be minimally invasive, avoiding formal dissections unless absolutely necessary. They are also a mirror to Peter Jones (1922–1995) who commissioned the drawings. Peter had both English and American fellowships of surgery and in 1960 was the first person to obtain the Australian fellowship in paediatric surgery. During his illustrious career he was on the council of the Royal Australian College of Surgeons (1987–95) and the Medical Defence Association of Victoria (1974–88), and was president of the Australian Association of Surgeons (1983–86). He was a legendary medical historian and a great raconteur, but will be remembered primarily as the author of the first three editions of what is now commonly called Jones’ clinical paediatric surgery, the ‘bible’ for medical students about surgical problems in childhood. description_tsim: The Green Plum is a favoured bush tucker across the Top End. It is eaten when the fruit ripen, the late build-up or early wet season, usually just before Christmas, the fruit remain green but are soft to touch. The fruit have a tangy taste a little like ginger-beer and contain a large, dark seed. Tiwi people use the Green Plum in several ways, the inner red bark is used as a dye for fibre-crafts and the green sap of new growth is used as glue to mix with paint to make it stay strong and vibrant. In other parts of the Northern Territory this species is used as a powerful medicine to treat toothaches, headaches, ringworm, insect bites, fever, eczema and other skin disorders. In some areas Green Plum is a calendar plant and flowering indicates the time when freshwater crocodiles are about to lay eggs. Austral Bracken (Mula) ferns are a perfect insect repellent, and were used to relieve stings and itching caused by bites or cuts. Curled tips of the fern have a nutty taste and can be eaten, once soaked for 24 hours and then dried; removal of the hairs is necessary to avoid irritation. Eating a large amount can cause stomach cancer, so do not over-consume. The roots and tubers are roasted and beaten into a paste that can be applied to the skin as a plaster and antiseptic for sores and burns. Root tea was used for the treatment of stomach cramps and sometimes diarrhoea, and a smoking of the fern and roots can soothe headaches. The plant can also be boiled and its natural oils extracted and turned into a wash to promote hair growth. You can bite the leaf to extract its juice and apply it to any irritation, or to minor cuts on the skin. The name Mula is derived from the Dja Dja Wurrung and Djab Wurrung languages.  © Kathrine Clarke

"Aboriginal life, from the everyday through to the most secret and sacred, is governed by a holistic spiritual belief system founded in the Dreaming, which I distil into two quintessential principles or values: respect and relationship. These principles underpin the Law of the land - that is, laws for living; how each person is connected to the great web of life through skin, kin, totems and Country. It involves ceremonial rituals that maintain ancestral stories and songlines. Because the land is the mother, we belong to her. We are charged with the responsibility to care for our Country, our mother, and all creatures, in perpetual seasonal cycles of renewal and regeneration. Birth, life, death: three pivotal transitions in human existence. Growing up into a woman with the capacity to give birth; becoming pregnant, nurturing a life within; giving birth, labouring to push forth a new life - these are all momentous and (hopefully) enriching and fulfilling experiences. The cycle of growth is made up of archetypal phases in a woman's life: growing from a girl-child into a young woman, then mother, and finally grandmother or crone. Being a mother is both gift and responsibility." Dr Vicki Couzens, 'The Women's: Carers, Advocates and Reformers' exhibition catalogue, 2019, excerpt, pp.5-10.

In 1914 the medical school celebrated its jubilee and in the New Year honours Allen was knighted. The profession presented him with his portrait by E. Phillips Fox; this was destroyed in the Wilson Hall fire in 1952.  Harry Brookes Allen (1854–1926) became the first Australian-born professor at the University of Melbourne in 1882, when a reform of the Medical School split the foundation chair of anatomy, pathology and physiology into two, with Allen being appointed professor of anatomy and pathology, and his teacher, the foundation professor George Britton Halford (1824-1910) retaining his first love, physiology. As well as serving as dean for extensive periods, Allen took on numerous positions as a medical administrator and government advisor, perhaps most importantly playing a major part in the introduction of Melbourne’s extensive sewerage system in the late nineteenth century. Photograph of female medical students (left to right) Christina Goode, Violet Plummer and Gertrude Mead in garden.  Gertrude Ella Mead(1867-1919), and  Violet May Plummer (1973-1962) graduated from medicine at the University of Melbourne  in 1897 and Christina Love Goode(1874 –1951) in 1898.All had commenced their studies in medicine in Adelaide.  Gertrude Ella Mead (1867-1919), trained as a nurse at the Adelaide Children's Hospital in 1890-91 and then studied medicine at the University of Adelaide; she graduated (M.B., B.S., 1897) from Melbourne. She went to  Britain in 1898 for postgraduate work and spent two years abroad, as resident physician at an English children's hospital, at a Dublin women's hospital and as a house surgeon at Leith, Scotland.  In 1901 she returned to Perth she was the third woman doctor to register in Western Australia and practised from her home at Harvest Terrace, Perth. Her paramount interest was in women's and children's welfare. She was appointed to the inaugural Senate of the University of Western Australia in 1912 as a medical representative; a fellow senator recalled her as 'a small thin woman with a mild voice and manner but a keen brain'.   Violet  May Plummer (1973-1962) matriculated in 1890. She gained her BSc. at the University of Adelaide in 1893 and passed her first year's medicine subjects the same year. She left for Melbourne in 1897 to complete the requirements for the Bachelor of Medicine rather than at Adelaide Hospital because of the "Hospital Row" (1896-1901).  Violet achieved second class passes, and later in 1898 she was appointed resident surgeon of the Melbourne Hospital then in 1899 resident surgeon in the infirmary department of the Women's Hospital, Melbourne.Violet Plummer never married.  Violet May Plummer was one of the first women from the University of Adelaide to graduate in medicine and in 1900 was the first woman General Practitioner to practise in Adelaide.  Christina Love Goode MB. BS. DPH. (1874 – 1951) married Alexander Krakowsky M.D. in 1914. She  studied medicine at Adelaide University for four years and completed her degree, with honours, at Melbourne in 1898. In 1906 she was appointed senior medical officer at the West Ham Infirmary, where she had been working for four years. This was the first occasion on which a woman has been made a senior officer at any infirmary in England. They returned to Adelaide in 1916 and took up positions at the Renmark hospital. She was prominent in the Girl Guide movement and a founding member of the Adelaide Lyceum Club.

' Dr. Crawford Henry Mollison, who was Victorian Government Pathologist for more than 50 years, died yesterday in Royal Melbourne Hospital at the age of 85. During his long official career Dr. Mollison appeared as witness in innumerable in quests and criminal trials to tell how, in medical terms, deceased persons met their death in circumstances ranging from accidents to murders. He was associated with investigations into most of the famous murder cases of his time, and was acknowledged as the Sir Bernard Salisbury of Australia. He became assistant pathologist at the old Melbourne Hospital 56 years ago. His activities at the City Morgue carried no salary, his remuneration being a fee of three guineas for each post-mortem examination. Among the famous cases on which his advice was sought were the "pyjama girl" mystery and the Deeming murder case.' The Age, 7 April 1949, p. 4.
